intransigence

in-TRAN-si-jents · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Intransigence is the refusal to compromise.

Years of intransigence on both sides doomed the peace talks -- neither delegation would give an inch on a single demand.

Example

The homeowners' association's intransigence over the fence height turned a simple disagreement into a three-year legal battle.

Intransigence names the stubborn, unyielding stance itself, usually in a negotiation or dispute where some flexibility is expected.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inflexibility: Inflexibility is a general unwillingness to bend or adapt — a schedule, a rule, or a person's habits can all be inflexible, with nothing at stake. Intransigence is sharper: a flat refusal to compromise in a negotiation or dispute, held while the standoff does real damage.

obstinacy: Obstinacy is a streak of personal temperament — digging in out of pride and refusing to change your mind, often over small matters, just to avoid giving in. Intransigence is a stance in a dispute: a sustained, deliberate refusal to compromise on the demands themselves.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flexibility: willingness to adapt or compromise

cooperation: working together willingly

Where it sits · how much harm the refusal causes — stubbornness → intransigence → fanaticism

stubbornness vs. intransigence: Stubbornness is far milder than intransigence: a little stubbornness over which restaurant to pick is harmless, while intransigence digs in on every demand until whole negotiations collapse.

fanaticism vs. intransigence: Fanaticism goes beyond even intransigence: intransigence refuses to compromise in a dispute, while fanaticism serves a cause with such blind devotion that any compromise at all feels like betrayal.

Word Choice

Intransigence describes a refusal to compromise in a negotiation or dispute -- a procedural, often political stance. Implacable describes a more personal, emotional refusal to forgive.
